newsitem.title: USA: Maryland mulls gangsta rap divestment.
newsitem.headline: Maryland mulls gangsta rap divestment.

text.p: Maryland, the first state to divest tobacco stocks from its employee pension system, is now considering selling off stocks in companies that produce "gangsta rap" music.
But the head of one company whose shares were targeted has said he wants to know what the pension board is doing to help ease the plight of disadvantaged people he said gave rise to the music.

The state's pension system board decided Wednesday to invite representatives of Universal Music owner Seagram Co Ltd and EMI Group Plc to attend its next meeting in August and respond to calls by state legislators to divest shares in the two firms, board spokesman Marvin Bond said Thursday.

"It's trying to make a business decision," Bond said of the board. He said the board had followed a similar, business-driven rationale in selling its tobacco stocks last year over concerns that increasing lawsuits and bad publicity could depress the shares.
The $23.7 billion state retirement and pension fund has about $14.5 million worth of Seagram stock and $17.1 million of EMI shares, Bond said.
Gangsta rap music has been criticized as having overly violent and misogynist lyrics, while defenders and performers say the music is an artistic interpretation of street and ghetto life.

In a letter to EMI Group Chairman Sir Colin Southgate in May, discussing state legislative efforts to ban investments in companies selling or producing gangsta rap recordings, retirement system director Peter Vaughn said EMI's involvement in rap music was "offensive and repulsive to the board and other public pension funds."

"In the exercise of the board's fiduciary responsibility we cannot sit idly by and allow a company in which we are a shareholder to profit from offensive corporate behavior," Vaughn said. He urged EMI to discuss with the pension board its rationale for being in the business.
Southgate said in a return letter the industry was working to strenghten parental advisories for explicit lyrics and that EMI retail outlets prohibited the sale of such music to minors.
But he said EMI has used a portion of its profits to aid disadvantaged groups and said he would like to learn about similar programs supported by the pension fund.
"Surely it is the socio-economic causes which created such (violent) environments that should be branded as obscene, not the music which results from it," Southgate said.
"We must all work together to understand and change the conditions which give rise to 'gangsta' rap," he said. "In my view, that is the only way to supress it."
